results.corrected_title: MIT, Microsoft and ECMWF machine learning correction roughly doubles skill of 2–6 week forecasts (Nature)
results.corrected_summary: A paper in Nature, 'Advancing subseasonal forecasting with machine learning', describes probabilistic bias correction (PBC). PBC is a low-cost, open-source machine learning layer that learns from a forecast model's past errors and corrects its output. Applied to ECMWF's models, it roughly doubled skill in the 2–6 week range. It also improved the debiased dynamical model on most targets, including 98% of precipitation, 92% of temperature and 91% of pressure targets. A submission using the method won first place in ECMWF's seasonal forecasting competition.
key_facts: Published in Nature; MIT News announced it on 14 October 2026 (an arXiv preprint, 2604.16238, came out earlier in 2026)
The method (probabilistic bias correction) roughly doubles the skill of ECMWF forecasts 2–6 weeks ahead; the paper says it doubles the modest skill of ECMWF's AI forecasting system
It improved 98% of precipitation, 92% of temperature and 91% of pressure targets for the debiased dynamical model
A submission using the method placed first in ECMWF's forecasting competition last year
Authors are from MIT (Judah Cohen), Microsoft (Lester Mackey and others), ECMWF, DTN, Harvard and the University of Toronto; the lead authors are Hannah Guan and Soukayna Mouatadid
The tool is open source and does not need a supercomputer to run
results.issues: The Nature page redirected to a login, so the paper's details come from search snippets and MIT News. A preprint was posted earlier in 2026, but the peer-reviewed Nature publication is the new event inside the window. The 98%/92% figures refer to improvements over the debiased dynamical model. The 'doubling' is described as relative to ECMWF's AI forecasting system.

results.corrected_title: Google Research grounds AI agents in physical lab robots for closed-loop molecule design
results.corrected_summary: Google Research described a system in which AI agents plan, run and evaluate experiments on lab robots. It uses VERID, a digital twin of the lab workcell built on the open-source PyLabRobot framework that tracks lab state and blocks invalid commands. In three rounds of aptamer design against α-thrombin, the hit rate rose from 0% to 26.0% to 42.1%, with 98.5% specificity. Against myoglobin, the agents revised their design rules and reached a 33.5% on-target hit rate. For FAP protein-binder design, a technique called epitope excision made each design cycle about 8.6x faster.
key_facts: Google Research blog post, 16 October 2026 (Pooja Rao, Petar Sirkovic, Annalisa Pawlosky)
VERID (VERified Infrastructure for Discovery Laboratories) is a digital twin of the workcell built on PyLabRobot, with virtual dry runs and hardware safety checks
α-thrombin aptamers: hit rate went 0% → 26.0% → 42.1% over three rounds, at 98.5% specificity
Myoglobin: 33.5% on-target hit rate and 72.4% specificity in round 3, after a drop in round 2
FAP binder design: epitope excision sped up each design cycle more than eightfold (8.6x); a human–agent hybrid nearly doubled the in-silico hit rate of a scientist working alone
results.issues: Only Google's own blog confirms this; there is no independent coverage and no peer review. All the numbers are Google's own and match the post. I did not check whether an earlier preprint exists.

results.corrected_title: Google says Gemini 4 Argon taught Apptronik's Apollo humanoid to play cornhole from one video
results.corrected_summary: Alongside the 13 October 2026 release of Gemini 4 Argon, Google DeepMind showed the model learning cornhole from one video of a person throwing bean bags. Argon built a simulation of the task and wrote its own simulation code, then controlled Apptronik's Apollo humanoid, which sank seven throws in a row after a few warm-ups. Google calls this approach 'Video-to-Sim-to-Real'. In a separate tabletop demo with two Franka robot arms, Argon built a simulation from one photo, and practising there raised the real-world success rate from 56% to 75%. All figures are Google's own internal demonstrations.
key_facts: Gemini 4 Argon was released on 13 October 2026; Google's robotics developer blog post is dated the same day
Cornhole demo: Argon learned from one video of a human and controlled Apptronik's Apollo humanoid, which made seven shots in a row after warm-up throws (per Google DeepMind)

The 4,500+ simulated episodes, the single-photo MuJoCo simulation and the 56% → 75% success rate (35 s → 24 s completion time) come from a separate demo with two Franka FR3 arms on table tasks, not the cornhole demo
Argon scored 87% on Google's ERQA embodied-reasoning benchmark
These are internal demonstrations and have not been independently verified
results.issues: The candidate mixes up two demos. The digital twin built from one photo, the 4,500+ simulated runs and the 56%→75% success rate come from a separate demo with two Franka FR3 arms on table tasks (Google Developers Blog). They do not belong to Apollo's cornhole demo. The cornhole demo and the seven-in-a-row result are confirmed by Google DeepMind's X post and several outlets. The Google developer blog does not mention cornhole itself. It does mention an 'Apollo 2' humanoid in a separate ball-throwing demo. The 13 October date is the Argon release and announcement date. All claims come from Google.
